title: Слово о пълку Игоревѣ
titleEn: The Tale of Igor's Campaign — VII: Vseslav of Polotsk
draftNote: Part VII — the movement turns from the roll-call appeal to Rus'’s great princes (part 6) to the ill-starred Polotsk line: Izyaslav Vasilkovich's death fighting the Lithuanians, and a reproach to his kinsmen for the feuds that first let raiders in. From there the poet tells, out of chronological order, the strange career of their forebear Vseslav Bryachislavich of Polotsk — his cast lot for the Kievan throne, his brief 1068–69 reign in Kiev, the earlier sack of Novgorod, the disastrous 1067 Battle of the Nemiga, and his legendary nightly turning into a wolf — closing on Boyan's old proverb that neither cunning nor skill escapes God's judgment, and a last turn to 'old Vladimir' and the disunited banners of Rurik and David.
source: Text: editio princeps — «Ироическая пѣснь о походѣ на половцовъ удѣльнаго князя Новагорода-Сѣверскаго Игоря Святославича», ed. A. I. Musin-Pushkin, Moscow, 1800 (public domain); via Russian Wikisource. 1800 orthography preserved. Prose sense-units at the edition's punctuation (no imposed verse lineation). Transliteration: scholarly Slavist romanization (ž š č c x; ě = ѣ; ŭ / ĭ = ъ / ь). Pronunciation: reconstructed late-12th-c. Old East Slavic (see slovo-audio doc); ж/ш/ц read hard by convention. Translations made fresh from the 1800 original.
about: Grief for the Polotsk princes' own ill fortune, and a backward look at the strangest figure in the poem. Izyaslav Vasilkovich falls fighting the Lithuanians, unaided by absent kinsmen; the poet lays the blame for outside raids on the Polotsk line's own feuds before turning to its ancestor, Vseslav Bryachislavich (d. 1101) — remembered in the chronicles, and here, as a sorcerer-prince who ruled by day and ran as a wolf by night. The poet recounts, in no fixed order, his lot cast for the Kievan throne, his seven-month reign there after the Kievans freed him in 1068, his earlier sack of Novgorod, and the ruinous 1067 Battle of the Nemiga, where the united Yaroslavichi defeated him — closing with Boyan's own proverb that no cunning, skill, or magic escapes divine judgment. As throughout the poem, several words here are genuine dark places found nowhere else in Old East Slavic (стрикусы, the corrupt «око ни», the crux «рози нося ... хоботы пашутъ») and are flagged as unresolved rather than translated with invented confidence — the poem survives in no manuscript (the single copy burned in 1812), so no reading here claims more certainty than the 1800 print itself supports.

sentences.t: Уже бо Сула не течетъ сребреными струями къ граду Переяславлю, и Двина болотомъ течетъ онымъ грознымъ Полочаномъ подъ кликомъ поганыхъ.
sentences.tr: Uže bo Sula ne tečetŭ srebrenymi strujami kŭ gradu Perejaslavlju, i Dvina bolotomŭ tečetŭ onymŭ groznymŭ Poločanomŭ podŭ klikomŭ poganyxŭ.
sentences.l: For already the Sula does not flow with silvery streams to the city of Pereyaslavl, and the Dvina flows as a bog for those dread men of Polotsk, under the cry of the pagans.
sentences.i: For the Sula no longer runs in silver streams to the city of Pereyaslavl, and the Dvina flows as a swamp for those dread Polotsk folk, under the war-cries of the heathen.
sentences.n: This movement opens directly on its theme: the Polotsk princely line descended from Vseslav, set against disaster on the Rus' rivers — the same device used to open part 4 ('Rus' mourns'). «сребреными струями» echoes the poem's recurring silver/blue-river imagery; a river not flowing as it should is an ill omen throughout the poem. «Полочаномъ», 'men of Polotsk,' names the people of Vseslav's own city; «поганыхъ», 'pagans,' most likely means the Lithuanians, who raided the Polotsk lands from the west — the very people the next sentence names a Rus' prince as fighting.

sentences.t: Единъ же Изяславъ сынъ Васильковъ позвони своими острыми мечи о шеломы Литовскія; притрепа славу дѣду своему Всеславу, а самъ подъ чрълеными щиты на кровавѣ травѣ притрепанъ Литовскыми мечи.
sentences.tr: Jedinŭ že Izjaslavŭ synŭ Vasilĭkovŭ pozvoni svoimi ostrymi meči o šelomy Litovskija; pritrepa slavu dědu svojemu Vseslavu, a samŭ podŭ črŭlenymi ščity na krovavě travě pritrepanŭ Litovskymi meči.
sentences.l: Alone, Izyaslav son of Vasilko rang out with his sharp swords upon the Lithuanian helmets; he struck [won] glory for his own grandfather Vseslav, but he himself, under crimson shields, on the bloody grass, was struck down by Lithuanian swords.
sentences.i: Izyaslav, son of Vasilko, alone rang his sharp swords against Lithuanian helmets and won fresh glory for his own grandfather Vseslav — but he himself, beneath crimson shields, was cut down on the bloody grass by Lithuanian blades.
sentences.n: «чрълеными», 'crimson' (of the shields), is spelled here with ъ. Part 1 itself varies: «чръленыя» with ъ (of the foxes yapping at shields) alongside «чрьлеными» with ь in its closing line — this unit's spelling matches the ъ-variant already seen in part 1, not a departure from it; part 6 does not use this word. A small, real spelling variant of the print, kept as printed.

sentences.t: И схоти ю на кровать, и рекъ: дружину твою, Княже, птиць крилы пріодѣ, а звѣри кровь полизаша.
sentences.tr: I sxoti ju na krovatĭ, i rekŭ: družinu tvoju, Knjaže, pticĭ krily priodě, a zvěri krovĭ polizaša.
sentences.l: And he desired her/it for a marriage-bed, and said: your druzhina, O Prince, the birds have covered with [their] wings, and the beasts have licked up [their] blood.
sentences.i: He had craved it as a man craves the marriage-bed — and word came: your men, O Prince, lie covered by the wings of birds, and the beasts have licked their blood.
sentences.n: A genuine dark place. The antecedent of «ю» ('her/it') and the speaker of «рекъ» ('said') are not given by the text. One proposed reading keeps Izyaslav as subject throughout — he had craved [glory, or battle itself] as ardently as a man craves the bed — but this is only one of several incompatible proposals, none dominant — before an unnamed voice, or the poet himself, reports the grim result: his retinue left as carrion, wings over it, its blood licked by beasts. We keep the 1800 wording and do not resolve who speaks or what «ю» is.

sentences.t: Не бысь ту брата Брячяслава, ни другаго Всеволода; единъ же изрони жемчюжну душу изъ храбра тѣла, чресъ злато ожереліе.
sentences.tr: Ne bysĭ tu brata Brjačjaslava, ni drugago Vsevoloda; jedinŭ že izroni žemčjužnu dušu izŭ xrabra těla, čresŭ zlato ožerelie.
sentences.l: There was not there a brother Bryachislav, nor another Vsevolod; alone he shed [his] pearly soul out of [his] brave body, through [his] golden collar.
sentences.i: No brother Bryachislav was at hand, no other Vsevolod — alone he let his pearl of a soul slip from his brave body, out through his golden collar.
sentences.n: Bryachislav and Vsevolod named here appear to be Izyaslav's own brothers (further sons of Vasilko), absent when he needed them; nothing beyond the text itself ties them to a securer identity, and none is asserted here. «изрони жемчюжну душу ... чресъ злато ожереліе» — 'shed his pearly soul ... through his golden collar' — is a striking, morbid image: the soul pictured as a pearl slipping out through the golden neck-ornament (ожереліе, a collar or torque marking princely rank), perhaps at the very place of the fatal wound. «бысь» is an aorist ('there was not', = modern 'не было').

sentences.t: Унылы голоси, пониче веселіе. Трубы трубятъ Городеньскіи.
sentences.tr: Unyly golosi, poniče veselie. Truby trubjatŭ Gorodenĭskii.
sentences.l: Doleful [are] the voices, mirth has drooped. The trumpets of Gorodno sound.
sentences.i: Voices have turned mournful, and gladness has drooped; the trumpets of Gorodno are sounding.
sentences.n: «пониче веселіе», 'mirth has drooped,' repeats almost verbatim the line that closes part 4 («а веселіе пониче») — the poet reusing his own refrain for another moment of grief. «Городеньскіи», 'of Gorodno,' most likely names the town on the Neman (later Grodno); whether this Gorodno was at the time held by a branch of Vseslav's own line, as sometimes proposed, is not securely established.

sentences.t: Ярославе, и вси внуце Всеславли уже понизить стязи свои, вонзить свои мечи вережени; уже бо выскочисте изъ дѣдней славѣ.
sentences.tr: Jaroslave, i vsi vnuce Vseslavli uže ponizitĭ stjazi svoi, vonzitĭ svoi meči vereženi; uže bo vyskočiste izŭ dědnej slavě.
sentences.l: Yaroslav, and all grandsons of Vseslav, now lower your own banners, plunge your own swords, [already] damaged, [into their sheaths]; for you have already sprung out from [your] grandfatherly glory.
sentences.i: Yaroslav, and all you grandsons of Vseslav — lower your banners now, sheathe your blunted swords; for you have already fallen away from your grandfather's glory.
sentences.n: The vocative «Ярославе» is itself uncertain — it may address one particular Polotsk prince of that name (perhaps another son of Vasilko, alongside Bryachislav and Vsevolod above), though some have wondered whether it conceals 'Ярославичи'; we keep the print's «Ярославе» and flag the uncertainty. «понизить»/«вонзить» are read here as infinitives (-ти contracted to -ть) used with imperative force — 'lower!', 'thrust/plunge!' (вонзити literally 'thrust into'; the destination, probably the scabbard, is left unstated by the verb) — though some editors instead take these as imperatives with a dropped -е (понизите/вонзите); neither reading is certain.

sentences.t: Вы бо своими крамолами начясте наводити поганыя на землю Рускую, на жизнь Всеславлю.
sentences.tr: Vy bo svoimi kramolami načjaste navoditi poganyja na zemlju Ruskuju, na žiznĭ Vseslavlju.
sentences.l: For you yourselves, by your own feuds, began to bring the pagans onto the Russian land, onto Vseslav's own patrimony.
sentences.i: For it was you yourselves, through your own quarrels, who first began bringing the pagans down upon the Russian land — upon Vseslav's own inheritance.
sentences.n: The poet lays the blame for outside incursions on the Polotsk princes' own «крамолы», 'feuds, strife' — the same charge levelled elsewhere in the poem at Oleg Svyatoslavich ('Gorislavich', part 3) for opening the door to the Polovtsians; a real echo of the poem's recurring complaint about princely disunity, though the two passages are not claimed to argue the identical point. «жизнь» here does not mean '(biological) life' but an older sense, 'estate, patrimony, livelihood' — Vseslav's own inherited domain.

sentences.t: Которое бо бѣше насиліе отъ земли Половецкыи!
sentences.tr: Kotoroe bo běše nasilie otŭ zemli Poloveckyi!
sentences.l: For what violence was there [ever] from the Polovtsian land!
sentences.i: And what real harm, after all, ever came from the Polovtsian land!
sentences.n: A bitter rhetorical exclamation, kept standing on its own as a complete outburst, unlike part 1's «О руская земле!», which opens a unit rather than standing alone in it. The poet implies that even the steppe raiders never did Rus' the harm that the princes' own feuds have done. «бѣше» is an imperfect ('there was, there used to be').

sentences.t: На седьмомъ вѣцѣ Трояни връже Всеславъ жребій о дѣвицю себѣ любу.
sentences.tr: Na sedĭmomŭ věcě Trojani vrŭže Vseslavŭ žrebij o děvicju sebě ljubu.
sentences.l: In Troyan's seventh century, Vseslav cast a lot for a maiden dear to himself.
sentences.i: In the seventh span of Troyan's time, Vseslav cast lots for a maiden he loved.
sentences.n: Троянь recurs here for the fourth time in the poem (parts 1, 3 and 4 all use it, always unidentified — a pagan god? the Roman emperor Trajan remembered as a legendary age? simply 'olden time' personified?). This is the poem's only place that numbers one of Troyan's 'ages' ('the seventh'), and no one has securely explained the count. «връже ... жребій о дѣвицю себѣ любу» is read two ways: literally, as an old marriage-divination (casting lots to win a bride); or allegorically, as Vseslav 'casting his lot' for the golden Kievan throne, figured as a beloved maiden — the sentences that follow do go on to tell of his leap to that very throne. Neither reading is certain, and none is chosen here.

sentences.t: Тъй клюками подпръся око ни, и скочи къ граду Кыеву, и дотчеся стружіемъ злата стола Кіевскаго.
sentences.tr: Tŭj kljukami podprŭsja oko ni, i skoči kŭ gradu Kyevu, i dotčesja stružiemŭ zlata stola Kievskago.
sentences.l: He propped himself on crutches [...], and leapt to the city of Kiev, and touched with a spear-shaft the golden throne of Kiev.
sentences.i: Propping himself on crutches, he leapt to the city of Kiev, and touched the golden Kievan throne with the shaft of his spear.
sentences.n: A genuine dark place: as printed, «око ни» does not parse as ordinary words, and it is kept exactly as the 1800 edition has it rather than silently mended (a common proposal reads the same letters differently, e.g. as a reference to a horse, but no reading commands consensus). «клюками подпръся», 'propped himself on crutches/staves,' is itself striking, and may hint at Vseslav's uncanny characterization rather than describe literal lameness. The sentence compresses a real event: in 1068, after the Yaroslavichi's defeat by the Polovtsians at the Alta, the Kievans rose up, freed the imprisoned Vseslav (he had been seized the year before, in 1067, after a truce sworn by kissing the cross) and made him prince of Kiev; «дотчеся стружіемъ злата стола» pictures him touching the throne with his spear-shaft, a gesture of taking possession. He held Kiev only about seven months before Izyaslav retook it with Polish help in 1069.

sentences.t: Скочи отъ нихъ лютымъ звѣремъ въ плъночи, изъ Бѣла-града, обѣсися синѣ мьглѣ, утръ же воззни стрикусы оттвори врата Нову-граду, разшибе славу Ярославу, скочи влъкомъ до Немиги съ Дудутокъ.
sentences.tr: Skoči otŭ nixŭ ljutymŭ zvěremŭ vŭ plŭnoči, izŭ Běla-grada, oběsisja sině mĭglě, utrŭ že vozzni strikusy ottvori vrata Novu-gradu, razšibe slavu Jaroslavu, skoči vlŭkomŭ do Nemigi sŭ Dudutokŭ.
sentences.l: He leapt away from them as a fierce beast at midnight, from Belgorod, hung himself in blue mist; and in the morning, having raised the strikusy, he opened the gates to Novgorod, shattered the glory of Yaroslav, [and] leapt as a wolf to the Nemiga from Dudutki.
sentences.i: By midnight he had bounded away from them like a savage beast, out of Belgorod, wrapping himself in blue mist; and by morning — raising the strikusy — he threw open Novgorod's gates, shattered Yaroslav's glory, and sprang as a wolf to the Nemiga from Dudutki.
sentences.n: This single sentence compresses several episodes of Vseslav's life without regard to their real order. «Скочи ... въ плъночи, изъ Бѣла-града» pictures his flight from Kiev — Belgorod, a real fortress-town just outside Kiev founded by Vladimir I, would lie on that route — an event of 1069, when Izyaslav retook Kiev; «обѣсися синѣ мьглѣ», 'hung himself in blue mist,' is the poem's clearest single image of his werewolf/shape-shifting nature. «стрикусы» is a genuine hapax legomenon of wholly unresolved meaning, left unglossed rather than guessed at. «оттвори врата Нову-граду, разшибе славу Ярославу» recalls the historical sack of Novgorod, which the Novgorod First Chronicle records Vseslav carrying out around 1066/1067, plundering the bells and furnishings of St. Sophia (built under Yaroslav the Wise, hence 'Yaroslav's glory') — an event that in real chronology comes before, not after, his imprisonment and reign in Kiev just described; the poem does not present these episodes in chronological order. «скочи влъкомъ до Немиги съ Дудутокъ» leads into the Battle of the Nemiga (1067); Dudutki is usually placed near Minsk, in the immediate vicinity of the Nemiga battle, though its exact site is not certain.

sentences.t: На Немизѣ снопы стелютъ головами, молотятъ чепи харалужными, на тоцѣ животъ кладутъ, вѣютъ душу отъ тѣла.
sentences.tr: Na Nemizě snopy steljutŭ golovami, molotjatŭ čepi xaralužnymi, na tocě životŭ kladutŭ, vějutŭ dušu otŭ těla.
sentences.l: At the Nemiga they lay sheaves with heads, they thresh with flails of kharalug [steel]; on the threshing-floor they lay down life; they winnow the soul from the body.
sentences.i: At the Nemiga, sheaves are laid with heads for grain, and they thresh with flails of kharalug steel; on the threshing-floor they lay down men's lives, winnowing soul from body.
sentences.n: The poem's most extended battle-as-harvest metaphor, for the historical Battle of the Nemiga (1067), where Vseslav was defeated by the united forces of the Yaroslavichi (Izyaslav, Svyatoslav and Vsevolod). Severed heads become sheaves, swords become threshing-flails, and the winnowing of grain becomes the parting of soul from body — the same харалугъ ('kharalug', a legendary hard steel) named of weapons elsewhere in the poem (parts 2–6). «Немизѣ» (loc. sg. of Немига) shows the regular consonant shift г → з before ѣ. All four clauses stand in the present tense, for vivid, ongoing horror.

sentences.t: Немизѣ кровави брезѣ не бологомъ бяхуть посѣяни, посѣяни костьми Рускихъ сыновъ.
sentences.tr: Nemizě krovavi brezě ne bologomŭ bjaxutĭ posějani, posějani kostĭmi Ruskixŭ synovŭ.
sentences.l: The Nemiga's bloody banks were not sown for good; [they were] sown with the bones of Russian sons.
sentences.i: The bloody banks of the Nemiga were sown, and not for any good — sown with the bones of Russia's sons.
sentences.n: Continues the sowing/harvest metaphor of the previous unit. «не бологомъ», 'not for good, inauspiciously,' recurs almost verbatim in part 6 («а древо не бологомъ листвіе срони») — the poet's set phrase for an ill omen. «бяхуть» is an old plural imperfect ('were').

sentences.t: Всеславъ Князь людемъ судяше, Княземъ грады рядяше, а самъ въ ночь влъкомъ рыскаше; изъ Кыева дорискаше до Куръ Тмутороканя; великому хръсови влъкомъ путь прерыскаше.
sentences.tr: Vseslavŭ Knjazĭ ljudemŭ sudjaše, Knjazemŭ grady rjadjaše, a samŭ vŭ nočĭ vlŭkomŭ ryskaše; izŭ Kyeva doriskaše do Kurŭ Tmutorokanja; velikomu xrŭsovi vlŭkomŭ putĭ preryskaše.
sentences.l: Prince Vseslav judged the people, arranged towns for princes, but himself by night coursed as a wolf; from Kiev he coursed as far as the cocks of Tmutorokan; as a wolf he cut across the path of the great Khors.
sentences.i: By day Prince Vseslav sat in judgment over the people and portioned out towns among the princes, but by night he ran as a wolf; from Kiev he raced to Tmutorokan before the cocks crowed there — running as a wolf, he cut across the very course of mighty Khors.
sentences.n: The poem's central statement of Vseslav's legend: a real prince of Polotsk (d. 1101) who, in folk memory, governed by day and turned werewolf by night — the Primary Chronicle records that his mother bore him through sorcery, with a knot bound to him at birth said to make him fierce. «до Куръ Тмутороканя» is usually read not as a place called 'Kur' but as 'до куръ', 'until the cocks [crowed]' — i.e. before dawn broke in Tmutorokan, a Rus' principality on the Taman peninsula, an impossible distance from Kiev to cover in one night; the 1800 print itself capitalizes «Куръ» as if it were a proper name, which may be why some readers have taken it as a place — but that capitalization is the printer's, not necessarily the lost manuscript's. «великому хръсови влъкомъ путь прерыскаше» is the poem's most famous crux about Vseslav: Хърсъ/Хорсъ (printed here lower-case despite naming a god) is one of the pagan idols Prince Vladimir set up in 980 per the Primary Chronicle, generally understood, though not with total certainty, as a solar deity; 'crossing great Khors's path' is usually taken to mean Vseslav, as wolf, outran or cut across the sun's own daily course before it could finish. The root рыска- ('course, range') repeats three times in this one sentence (рыскаше, дорискаше, прерыскаше), binding Vseslav's wolf-running together; the imperfects (судяше, рядяше, рыскаше) picture habitual, repeated action.

sentences.t: Тому въ Полотскѣ позвониша заутренюю рано у Святыя Софеи въ колоколы: а онъ въ Кыевѣ звонъ слыша.
sentences.tr: Tomu vŭ Polotskě pozvoniša zautrenjuju rano u Svjatyja Sofei vŭ kolokoly: a onŭ vŭ Kyevě zvonŭ slyša.
sentences.l: For him, in Polotsk, they rang matins early at St. Sophia's, in the bells: but he, in Kiev, heard the ringing.
sentences.i: For him, early matins were rung out in Polotsk at St. Sophia's bells — yet he, in Kiev, heard the ringing.
sentences.n: One more mark of Vseslav's uncanny nature: he hears, from Kiev, bells ringing hundreds of miles away in Polotsk. The Cathedral of St. Sophia in Polotsk — built, like its namesakes in Kiev and Novgorod, in imitation of Constantinople's Hagia Sophia, and traditionally associated with Vseslav's own patronage — still stands today (rebuilt in the 18th century after later damage). «позвониша» repeats the same verb root used of Izyaslav's clashing swords in unit 2 («позвони ... о шеломы»), the poem's 'ringing' carried from battle-clang to church bells. «позвониша» and «слыша» are aorist forms.

sentences.t: Аще и вѣща душа въ друзѣ тѣлѣ, нъ часто бѣды страдаше.
sentences.tr: Ašče i věšča duša vŭ druzě tělě, nŭ často bědy stradaše.
sentences.l: Although [his] prophetic soul [was] in another body, yet often he suffered misfortunes.
sentences.i: Though his was a prophetic soul lodged in another kind of body, still he often suffered misfortune.
sentences.n: A difficult, much-discussed line. «вѣща душа», 'prophetic/wise soul,' ties back to the chronicle legend of Vseslav's sorcerous birth; «въ друзѣ тѣлѣ», 'in another['s]/a different body,' has been read variously — perhaps a poetic way of saying his more-than-human soul was housed in ordinary mortal flesh, perhaps a glancing reference to his shape-shifting into an animal body, perhaps something else again; none of these is asserted as settled. Whatever its exact sense, the line's point is plain: despite his magical gifts, Vseslav's life was one of repeated setbacks — imprisonment, defeat at Nemiga, a brief and lost reign in Kiev.

sentences.t: Тому вѣщей Боянъ и пръвое припѣвку смысленый рече: ни хытру, ни горазду, ни птицю горазду, суда Божіа не минути.
sentences.tr: Tomu věščej Bojanŭ i pŭrvoe pripěvku smyslenyj reče: ni xytru, ni gorazdu, ni pticju gorazdu, suda Božia ne minuti.
sentences.l: To this the prophetic Boyan, wisely, once already said as a refrain: neither to the cunning, nor to the skilled, nor to the skilled bird, [is it possible] to avoid the judgment of God.
sentences.i: Of this the prophetic Boyan, wisely, had already sung out this refrain: not the cunning man, not the skilled man, not even the skilled bird, can escape the judgment of God.
sentences.n: The poem's latest invocation of Boyan by name, following those in the proem and twice already in part 1, and its clearest quotation of one of his sayings, offered as an old, already-known «припѣвку», 'refrain,' rather than freshly composed. The triad хытру / горазду / птицю горазду ('cunning man / skilled man / skilled bird') builds to a climax — even a bird's cunning, an apt image right after two units built on Vseslav's own wolf-legend — cannot outrun divine judgment; a fitting verdict on a whole career of clever, uncanny escapes. «вѣщей», 'prophetic,' is the same epithet given Boyan in part 1 («вѣщей Бояне, Велесовь внуче!»).

sentences.t: О! стонати Руской земли, помянувше пръвую годину, и пръвыхъ Князей.
sentences.tr: O! stonati Ruskoj zemli, pomjanuvše pŭrvuju godinu, i pŭrvyxŭ Knjazej.
sentences.l: O! [there is nothing left but] to groan, O Russian land, having remembered the first age, and the first princes.
sentences.i: O, Russian land — nothing is left but to groan, remembering an earlier age, and its earlier princes!
sentences.n: The interjection «О!» is kept together with the clause it introduces, rather than left to stand alone, since the two form one outcry (compare part 1's «Длъго.», folded into its following sentence). «стонати» is an infinitive used exclamatorily/impersonally ('there is nothing to do but groan'). This turns the poem toward its closing image, 'old Vladimir' — echoing part 1's own opening, «отъ стараго Владимера до нынѣшняго Игоря» ('from old Vladimir to the present Igor'), naming the same figure by the same epithet.

sentences.t: Того стараго Владиміра не льзѣ бѣ пригвоздити къ горамъ Кіевскимъ: сего бо нынѣ сташа стязи Рюриковы, а друзіи Давидовы; нъ рози нося имъ хоботы пашутъ, копіа поютъ на Дунаи.
sentences.tr: Togo starago Vladimira ne lĭzě bě prigvozditi kŭ goramŭ Kievskimŭ: sego bo nyně staša stjazi Rjurikovy, a druzii Davidovy; nŭ rozi nosja imŭ xoboty pašutŭ, kopia pojutŭ na Dunai.
sentences.l: That old Vladimir it was not possible to nail down to the Kievan hills: for now instead there stand the banners of Rurik, and others of David; but, [each] bearing [its own], their banner-tails flap, [their] spears sing on the Danube.
sentences.i: That old Vladimir could not be nailed down forever to the Kievan hills — instead, the banners standing there now are Rurik's, and others David's; but their pennants flutter apart, and their spears sing far off on the Danube.
sentences.n: 'Old Vladimir' most likely repeats the figure named at the very start of part 1, probably Vladimir Monomakh (d. 1125), remembered here as a strong ruler who — unlike now — could be pictured as permanently fixed at Kiev; spelled here «Владиміра» (with і), unlike «Владимера» (with е) in part 1's opening line naming the same man — another small, real spelling variant of the 1800 print, kept as printed. «не льзѣ бѣ», 'it was not possible' (льзѣ, an old impersonal predicate + бѣ, imperfect of быти), is the ancestor of modern Russian's frozen 'нельзя'. Рюриковы and Давидовы are Rurik and David Rostislavich, the Smolensk-line princes jointly appealed to in part 6; here their banners stand apart rather than together, an image of disunity persisting even among allies. «рози нося имъ хоботы пашутъ» is itself a genuine crux with more than one proposed reading: some editors reconstruct «розно ся ... пашуть», 'their banner-tails ('хоботы') flutter apart/separately'; others take «рози» closer to the printed letters, as 'horns' — a possible echo of the biblical idiom of the 'horn' as an emblem of pride or power. Neither is asserted here as correct; the 1800 print is kept exactly. The closing Danube recalls the Danube named in part 6 for Yaroslav Osmomysl's Galician power; whether a specific campaign is meant, or the poet simply reaches for a distant edge of the Rus' world to close on, the text does not say.
